sixtySeconds.whatItDoes: Strix is an open-source AI penetration testing tool. Its autonomous agents run your app, look for security vulnerabilities, and confirm them with working proofs of concept, then suggest fixes.
sixtySeconds.problem: Traditional scanners produce many false positives, and manual pentests take weeks. Strix uses AI agents with real security tools to find and validate issues quickly, and can run in CI to block insecure code before release.
whoFor: Security teams speeding up penetration tests
Teams adding security checks to CI/CD
sixtySeconds.whyChoose: Choose it for validated, developer-friendly security findings from a local CLI with your own LLM key. Only point it at systems you own or have written permission to test.
requirements: An LLM API key from a supported provider (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and others)

overview: Strix runs teams of AI agents equipped with an HTTP interception proxy, an automated browser, a shell, a Python exploit sandbox, reconnaissance tools and static and dynamic analysis. They test for the OWASP Top 10 and more: access control, injection, SSRF, XSS, business logic, authentication and API issues.

Findings include proofs of concept and remediation guidance, and results are saved to strix_runs/ and viewable in a local web dashboard with strix view. Strix can also run in GitHub Actions to scan pull requests, and installs as skills for Claude Code, Cursor and Codex.

The open-source version runs locally with Docker and your own LLM key. Strix Cloud and Enterprise are paid hosted offerings with autofix pull requests, continuous testing and compliance reports. The README stresses authorized use only: you are responsible for permission and legal compliance.

troubleshooting.solution: It pulls the sandbox Docker image automatically on first use.
Run strix --update, or the matching pipx, uv or pip upgrade command it prints.
Make sure Docker is running and STRIX_LLM and LLM_API_KEY are set.
